title: Energy Use
in30Seconds: Energy use is how society draws on primary sources — petroleum, natural gas, coal, nuclear, and renewables — to run transportation, industry, and buildings. Most of that energy still comes from fossil fuels, and much of it never reaches a useful task: it leaves as waste heat. This lesson separates primary energy from electricity, sorts consumption by sector, sets the units straight, and shows where the energy actually goes.
whyItMatters: Almost every environmental problem — climate change, air pollution, resource depletion — traces back to how much energy people use and where it comes from. Reading energy statistics correctly is a prerequisite for every later topic in this field: you cannot evaluate a climate target, a renewable-energy claim, or an efficiency policy without knowing whether a number describes primary energy or electricity, capacity or generation, power or energy. Getting the vocabulary and the scale right lets you tell a real change from a rounding error, judge which sectors matter most, and see why a large share of primary energy is lost before it does any work.
learningObjectives: Distinguish primary energy from electricity, a secondary energy carrier.
Identify the four end-use sectors and describe the current U.S. energy mix with dated figures.
Define the core energy units (joule, watt, watt-hour, kWh, BTU, quad) and distinguish power from energy.
Explain energy intensity and what decoupling energy use from GDP means.
Analyze where primary energy is lost as rejected energy rather than delivered as a service.

collegeVersion.heading: Primary energy versus electricity
collegeVersion.body: Primary energy is energy in the form nature supplies it: crude oil and petroleum products, natural gas, coal, uranium for nuclear reactors, and renewable flows such as sunlight, wind, flowing water, and biomass. Electricity is not on that list. Electricity is a secondary energy carrier — it has to be generated from a primary source before it can be used, and generating and delivering it loses energy along the way. This distinction governs how energy statistics are read. When the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) reports that the United States consumed about 96 quadrillion British thermal units (quads) of primary energy in 2025, that total counts the coal, gas, uranium, and sunlight going into power plants, not the kilowatt-hours coming out. A renewable 'share' of electricity is therefore a different number from a renewable share of total primary energy, and confusing the two is one of the most common errors in energy reporting. Whenever you meet an energy figure, the first question is which layer it describes: the primary source, the electricity generated, or the energy actually delivered to a task.

collegeVersion.heading: The current mix and where energy is used
collegeVersion.body: For 2025, EIA's consumption-by-source-and-sector data put U.S. primary energy at roughly 96 quads, split as petroleum 35.9 quads (37%), natural gas 34.6 quads (36%), coal 8.7 quads (9%), renewables 8.8 quads (9%), and nuclear 8.2 quads (9%). Fossil fuels — petroleum, natural gas, and coal together — supply about 82% of the total; renewables and nuclear make up the remaining 18%. That fossil majority has held for decades even as coal has fallen sharply and renewables have grown. EIA sorts consumption into four end-use sectors plus the electric power sector. Counting the primary energy each end-use sector burns directly, transportation used 28.2 quads (37%), industry 26.6 quads (35%), residential 11.8 quads (15%), and commercial 9.9 quads (13%) in 2025. Residential and commercial look small in this direct view because most of the energy those buildings use arrives as electricity, whose primary inputs are counted in the power sector. EIA's alternative accounting distributes electricity and its losses back to the sectors that buy it, which raises the building sectors' shares. Both slices are correct; you just have to know which one a chart is showing.

collegeVersion.heading: Units: energy, power, and the ones you will meet
collegeVersion.body: The SI unit of energy is the joule (J). Power is the rate of using energy: one watt (W) is one joule per second. That single relationship, energy equals power multiplied by time, prevents most unit mistakes. A watt is power; a watt-hour (Wh) is energy — the amount used by a one-watt device running for one hour, equal to 3,600 joules. The kilowatt-hour (kWh), 1,000 watt-hours, is the unit on an electricity bill; one kWh equals 3.6 megajoules. The British thermal unit (BTU) is a customary energy unit, about 1,055 joules, roughly the heat to raise one pound of water one degree Fahrenheit; one kWh is about 3,412 BTU. At national scale EIA uses the quad, one quadrillion (10¹⁵) BTU, so it can add oil, gas, coal, and electricity on one axis. The recurring error is treating a power rating as if it were energy: a '1,500-watt heater' tells you nothing about consumption until you multiply by the hours it runs. Capacity (installed watts) and generation (energy actually produced) are the same trap at grid scale.

collegeVersion.heading: Energy intensity, decoupling, and rejected energy
collegeVersion.body: Energy intensity is energy consumed per unit of economic output — for a country, total primary energy divided by real GDP. When intensity falls, an economy produces more value from each unit of energy. U.S. energy intensity has declined steadily since the early 1970s, driven by efficiency gains and a shift toward less energy-hungry service industries; EIA's Annual Energy Outlook 2020 projected U.S. energy consumption growing about 0.3% per year through 2050 while GDP grows about 1.9%, an average 1.5% annual fall in intensity. Growth outpacing energy use is called decoupling. Intensity is not the same as total emissions or total energy, which can still rise even as intensity falls. Finally, much primary energy never becomes a useful service. Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's flow chart for 2023 estimated U.S. energy at 93.6 quads, of which only 32.1 quads became energy services and 61.5 quads left as rejected energy — mostly waste heat from combustion. Electricity shows the same pattern in EIA's 2025 data: of the energy the power sector consumed, about 59% was lost and only 41% reached customers. Some of this loss is a hard limit of thermodynamics; some is a target for efficiency.

vocabulary.definition: Energy captured directly from a natural source — fossil fuels, nuclear fuel, sunlight, wind, water, biomass — before any conversion.
A form of energy produced from a primary source and used to move energy to where it is needed; electricity and hydrogen are examples.
One of the categories — transportation, industrial, residential, commercial — that EIA uses to group who consumes energy.
The SI unit of energy; one watt of power sustained for one second.
The SI unit of power, equal to one joule per second; a rate of energy use, not an amount.
A unit of energy equal to one kilowatt used for one hour, or 3.6 megajoules; the standard unit on electricity bills.
A customary unit of energy, about 1,055 joules; roughly the heat needed to raise one pound of water by one degree Fahrenheit.
One quadrillion (10^15) BTU; the scale EIA uses to report national and global energy consumption.
Energy consumed per unit of economic output, such as primary energy per real dollar of GDP.
Primary energy that does not become a useful service and instead leaves the system, mostly as waste heat from combustion and conversion.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Energy comes out of the ground or the sky as fuel, sunlight, or wind — that is primary energy. Electricity is different: it has to be made from those primary sources, and making and shipping it wastes a big chunk along the way. When people add up all the energy a country uses, they count the fuel going in, not just the electricity coming out. They also sort it by who uses it: vehicles, factories, and buildings. A watt tells you how fast something uses energy; a kilowatt-hour tells you how much it used. And a surprising amount of the energy we start with never does a useful job — it slips away as heat.
eli10.analogy: Think of primary energy like the whole paycheck and electricity like the cash you actually get to spend after taxes and fees are taken out. The paycheck (the fuel) is bigger than the spendable cash (the delivered energy), because generating and delivering electricity skims a lot off the top as lost heat.
eli10.analogyLimits: The paycheck analogy captures the losses but not the reasons. Taxes are a policy choice that could be changed; a large part of energy loss is fixed by the laws of thermodynamics — any heat engine must reject some heat and can never convert all fuel to work. And unlike money, energy is never destroyed; the 'lost' energy still exists, just as low-temperature heat too diffuse to do useful work.

workedExample: Suppose a 1,500-watt space heater runs 3 hours a day for 30 days. Start from energy equals power times time. Convert the rating to kilowatts: 1,500 W = 1.5 kW. Energy used = 1.5 kW × 3 h/day × 30 days = 135 kWh for the month. At an electricity price of $0.17 per kWh, that is 135 × $0.17 = $22.95. To see the same energy in other units: 135 kWh × 3.6 MJ/kWh = 486 megajoules, and 135 kWh × 3,412 BTU/kWh ≈ 460,600 BTU. For scale, a typical U.S. home purchased about 10,791 kWh of electricity in 2022 (EIA), roughly 899 kWh a month — so this one heater running a few hours a day is a noticeable slice of a household's electricity. Notice the heater's 1,500-watt label alone told you nothing about cost; only multiplying power by time produced an amount of energy.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating electricity as a primary energy source.
commonMistakes.correction: Electricity is a secondary carrier generated from primary sources like gas, coal, nuclear, or sunlight. A renewable share of electricity is a different figure from a renewable share of total primary energy.
A watt is power (a rate); a watt-hour is energy (an amount). Multiply power by the hours of operation to get energy. A device's wattage alone does not tell you how much it consumes.

Installed capacity (watts or GW) is how much a plant could produce at full output; generation (Wh or TWh) is how much energy it actually produced over time. A high-capacity plant that rarely runs generates little.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming most primary energy reaches a useful task.
commonMistakes.correction: A large share leaves as rejected energy, mainly waste heat. For 2023, LLNL estimated only about a third of U.S. primary energy became useful energy services.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading falling energy intensity as falling total energy or emissions.
commonMistakes.correction: Energy intensity is energy per dollar of GDP. It can decline while total energy use and total emissions still rise, if the economy grows faster than intensity falls.

compareContrast.distinction: Primary energy is the raw source going into the system; electricity is a secondary carrier made from it, with substantial conversion and delivery losses in between.
Power is the rate of using energy at an instant; energy is power accumulated over time. Energy = power × time.
Capacity is the maximum rate a plant can produce (installed watts); generation is the energy it actually produced over a period (watt-hours).
Intensity is energy per unit of GDP and can fall while total energy use rises; total use is the absolute quantity consumed.

keyTakeaway: Read every energy figure by asking which layer it names — primary source, electricity, or delivered service — and whether it is power or energy. Fossil fuels still supply about 82% of U.S. primary energy (EIA, 2025), and most primary energy is lost as waste heat before it does useful work.

questionBank.prompt: Why is electricity classified as a secondary energy carrier rather than a primary energy source?
options: It must be generated from a primary source such as gas, coal, nuclear, or sunlight before it can be used
It is measured in kilowatt-hours instead of quads
It is used only by the residential and commercial sectors
It is a renewable resource that never runs out
questionBank.explanation: Electricity does not occur as a usable natural stock; it is produced from primary sources, with losses during generation and delivery, which is exactly what makes it secondary. The unit it is measured in is irrelevant to the classification. It is used across all sectors, and it is not itself renewable — its inputs may or may not be.
questionBank.skill: Distinguishing primary energy from secondary carriers

questionBank.prompt: According to EIA data for 2025, roughly what share of total U.S. primary energy consumption came from fossil fuels (petroleum, natural gas, and coal combined)?
options: About 40%
About 60%
About 82%
About 98%
questionBank.explanation: EIA's 2025 source-and-sector data give petroleum 37%, natural gas 36%, and coal 9%, summing to about 82%; renewables (9%) and nuclear (9%) make up the rest. 40% and 60% understate the fossil majority, and 98% ignores the roughly 18% from nuclear and renewables.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the current U.S. primary energy mix with its date

questionBank.prompt: A 1,200-watt appliance runs for 2 hours. How much energy does it use, and which quantity is the '1,200 watts'?
options: 1,200 watt-hours of energy; the rating is an amount of energy
2,400 watts of energy; the rating is an amount of energy
600 watt-hours of energy; the rating is a unit of time
2.4 kilowatt-hours of energy; the rating is a measure of power
questionBank.explanation: Energy = power × time = 1.2 kW × 2 h = 2.4 kWh (2,400 Wh). The 1,200-watt figure is power, the rate of energy use, not an amount of energy or a time. Options that call the rating an 'amount of energy' confuse power with energy, and 600 Wh miscomputes the arithmetic.
questionBank.skill: Applying energy = power × time and distinguishing power from energy

questionBank.prompt: A country's real GDP grows 2% in a year while its total primary energy use rises 0.3%. What has most clearly happened to its energy intensity, and what does that imply about total energy use?
options: Energy intensity rose, and total energy use fell
Energy intensity fell, yet total energy use still rose
Energy intensity and total energy use both fell
Energy intensity stayed constant because GDP and energy both grew
questionBank.explanation: Energy intensity is energy per unit of GDP. GDP grew faster (2%) than energy use (0.3%), so energy per dollar fell — that is decoupling. But energy use still rose in absolute terms (0.3%), showing that falling intensity does not by itself mean falling total energy. Intensity did not stay constant, since the two grew at different rates.
questionBank.skill: Interpreting energy intensity and decoupling from GDP

questionBank.prompt: Lawrence Livermore's 2023 flow chart estimated U.S. energy at 93.6 quads, of which about 32.1 quads became energy services and 61.5 quads became rejected energy. What does the rejected-energy figure primarily represent?
options: Waste heat lost during combustion and energy conversion
Energy exported to other countries
Renewable energy that went unused because storage was full
An accounting error that should be subtracted from the total
questionBank.explanation: Rejected energy is primary energy that never becomes a useful service, mostly low-grade waste heat from burning fuels and running heat engines — partly a thermodynamic limit. It is not exports, not idle renewables, and not a mistake; it is a real, measured category showing that only about a third of U.S. primary energy delivered useful services in 2023.
questionBank.skill: Interpreting rejected energy and overall system efficiency
